title: RZD • Sanatorium Booking System
subtitle: Turning a complex internal process into a predictable booking flow
coverAlt: RZD sanatorium and resort booking service cover

facts.label: scope
value: UI system for a reusable internal service

facts.label: audience
value: Users with different eligibility and booking conditions

facts.label: role
value: Product Designer across system behavior, interaction logic, and UI

facts.label: focus
value: Predictability, trust, and repeat usage under real operational constraints

value.text: The sanatorium & resort booking service is one of the internal services within the RZD employee ecosystem.
It operates similarly to a booking platform, but includes additional constraints:
The service covers 500+ resorts nationwide and is available to employees and their families.
Despite its value, it remained underutilized due to complexity and lack of trust.
The service was not broken in terms of functionality — it was broken in terms of predictability.
Employees could technically complete a booking, but the process required constant interpretation.
Users had to figure out:

items: which resorts were available to them
whether the effort would lead to a real outcome

value.text: This created a specific behavioral pattern.
Users entered with intent, but quickly lost confidence:

items: selection loops forced them to restart
the process felt like a "black box"

value.text: Even successful bookings did not build trust.
The system did not answer: “Can I rely on this next time?”
The failure was not in conversion — it was in retention.
Users treated the service as a one-time, risky interaction.
The redesign had to operate within strict limitations:

items: multiple audience types within one flow

value.text: The challenge was not to reduce complexity, but to make it understandable.
The service was reframed as a behavioral system.
Not:
search → book → done
But:
experience → trust → return → habit
The goal was not to complete bookings, but to make the service reusable.
The issue was not that the process was complex.
It was that the system did not help users understand that complexity.
The experience varied depending on:
From the user’s perspective, the system behaved unpredictably.
This made every interaction feel like a one-time attempt.
The problem became behavioral: the system failed to build trust.
The solution required making system logic visible and structured.
Once the problem was reframed, the focus shifted from UI to system behavior.
Instead of designing a single flow, the service was mapped as overlapping journeys.
Each journey represented a different user type:
This revealed:
The goal was not simplification, but legibility.

value.alt: Information architecture and audience-specific journeys for the sanatorium booking service
value.caption: Before designing screens, I mapped the service as a decision system: information architecture, user types, and expectation failures were laid out explicitly so the interface could respond to real behavioral divergence instead of hiding it under one generic flow.

value.alt: Wireframe set for search, filtered results, card, and booking form
value.caption: These wireframes were not visual drafts. They were a way to test whether the service stages remained legible as one coherent logic: entry, comparison, selection, eligibility, and booking had to connect without forcing users to reinterpret the system at each step.

value.alt: Readable service flow with loops and decision points
value.caption: I treated the service as a set of overlapping journeys with shared rules and different failure points. That made it possible to design for real loops, branch conditions, and recovery paths instead of pretending the booking process was linear.

value.text: Each decision reduces uncertainty and supports repeat behavior.
Comparison
Replaced manual tab comparison with structured comparison.
Improves decision confidence (Experience).

value.caption: The comparison layer was designed to reduce interpretation work. Instead of making users open multiple pages and reconstruct differences manually, the system externalized the decision criteria and turned comparison into a supported action.

value.text: Early eligibility
Moved eligibility logic before booking.
Reduces failed attempts (Trust).
Loop handling
Made loops explicit and recoverable.
Removes frustration (Experience + Trust).
System transparency
Introduced clear states, steps, and expectations.
Enables predictability (Trust → Return).

value.alt: Booking flow with explicit steps and expectations
value.caption: The booking form was used to expose system logic early: constraints, eligibility, required inputs, and next steps became part of the interface. This reduced the feeling of a black box and made submission feel like a predictable step rather than a risky guess.

value.text: Reduced external dependency
Moved critical info into UI.
Reduces calls, increases reliance on system (Trust).
Repeat usage
Added re-entry via history and simplified flows.
Enables Return → Habit.
System structure
Defined consistent stages: discovery → comparison → eligibility → booking → approval → outcome.
Makes system learnable.

value.alt: Main page of the sanatorium booking service with structured entry points and curated selections
value.caption: The main page was redesigned as a structured entry point, not a decorative homepage. Its job was to orient users, shorten the path to relevant options, and reduce the cognitive cost of entering a complex service for the first time.

value.text: To support the UI layer, I also built a minimal viable design system with typography, spacing, and core interface elements. It was structured using Atomic Design principles so that the service could stay visually consistent while the interaction model remained scalable.

value.alt: Design system foundations and component structure for the sanatorium booking service
value.caption: I built the UI on top of a minimal but explicit system of typography, spacing, and reusable interface elements. That was important not for visual polish, but for operational consistency: repeated states, steps, and content patterns had to behave as one learnable product.

value.text: The service became a structured system that explains itself.
Users can:
The system no longer requires interpretation.

value.alt: Status tracking interface for booking progress
value.caption: Trust does not end at submission. This status layer was designed to keep the system legible after the user acts, so waiting, approval, and document handling remain understandable instead of becoming a silent operational gap.

value.alt: Detailed booking status and outcome tracking
value.caption: Outcome visibility was treated as part of the service itself. By making progress, decisions, and next actions explicit, the system could close the loop properly and give users a reason to rely on it again in the future.

value.text: The service shifted from a one-time interaction to repeatable behavior.
Users move from: “I don’t want to deal with this again” to: “I can use this next year”.
Results:
Repeat Usage Share
The percentage of users who return to the service.
This reflects trust, value, and long-term adoption.
